newsitem.title: QATAR: Qatar Rasgas bond said competitively priced.
newsitem.headline: Qatar Rasgas bond said competitively priced.

text.p: Ras Laffan LNG Co's $1.2 billion December bond issue carried an all-in cost of 8.65 percent compared to 9.60 percent in a parallel $1.35 billion bank and export facility, a manager at underwriter Goldman Sachs said.

The Rasgas bond, to finance a 10 million tonne annual capacity liquefied natural gas plant in Qatar, was the largest project-financing bond issued in capital markets and the first bond issue for a Middle East project, Goldman Sachs vice president of investment banking Daniel Lief said.
"The capital markets are much less concerned about political or regional risk and volatility in the Middle East than many people had expected," Lief said in a paper to a gas conference.

Rasgas is 63 percent owned by the state's Qatar General Petroleum Corp (QGPC). Mobil has 25 percent, Itochu and Nissho Iwai have 3.5 percent each and an undeclared South Korean firm has reserved a five percent stake.
Originally, the bond was to be for $400 million, but it was increased to $1.2 billion after heavy market interest.

Lief said the issue's first $400 million tranche had a ten year maturity with an average life of seven years at a coupon of 7.628 percent. The second $800 million tranche, with maturity of 17.5 years, has an average 15-year life at 8.294 percent.

The issue attracted 70 investors with the average size of investment at $15-20 million. The largest investment was $125 million. U.S. investors accounted for 82 percent of bond financing for the Qatar gas export project, Lief added.

Half the issue was taken up by investment advisers and pension funds, mutual funds took 23 percent, insurance companies 15 percent and banks and other institutions the remaining 12 percent, Lief's paper showed.

Rasgas has raised $450 million through syndicated loans and $900 million through U.S., British and Italian export credit agency facilities. QGPC has provided $600 million and Mobil $250 million in equity, bringing in a total $3.4 billion necessary for the first two production trains of the plant.
First-phase exports for the project, using the reserves of Qatar's North Field, are expected in 1999.
